life-027 · development · fictional age 16

Written life first, then interpreted by a separate response author without the engine or results. These are synthetic checks. There is no correct career answer key.

Life from age 4 to 16

I have had room to follow questions for a long time, which I appreciate. I also want to know how I do when the room is full of people who do not already know my family or how I learned something.

  • family: Lives with parents and two brothers on a small acreage; grandmother visits often.
  • finances: Moderate income; one parent works remotely and one manages local accounts.
  • geography: Outside Canyon, Texas.
  • cultureLanguages: English; secular household with close ties to neighbors of differing beliefs.
  • school: Homeschooled through a cooperative with shared science and literature classes.
  • accessOpportunities: Flexible schedule, nearby community college, and limited large-group experience.
  • Age 4–5

    In 2014, Cora followed family goats around the yard and invented stories about their rivalries. She disliked formal worksheets but asked her parents to write down long explanations of what the animals had supposedly discussed.

  • Age 6–7

    At six, she began home lessons and a weekly cooperative class. During 2017, she enjoyed reading with older children, while group games confused her when other students changed rules they assumed everyone already knew.

  • Age 8–9

    In 2018, Cora took a community theater class and discovered that rehearsed conflict could be funny. She liked performing a strong-minded character but remained reluctant to speak when adults asked the real group to make decisions.

  • Age 10–11

    During 2020, her academic routine changed less than many friends’ routines did. She missed cooperative meetings and began exchanging hand-drawn puzzle letters with another student, making them increasingly difficult until neither could solve the last set.

  • Age 12–13

    At twelve, Cora tried a supervised livestock project and liked tracking feed and growth more than show preparation. In 2023, she also started reading essays that challenged opinions common in her family’s social circle.

  • Age 14–15

    Across 2024 and 2025, she joined a public-library discussion group and helped stage a children’s play. She found disagreement easier when participants had read the same text, but sometimes mistook a confident speaking style for a stronger argument.

  • Age 16

    At sixteen in 2026, Cora is exploring Texas dual-credit classes and a short residential literature program. She wants experience in a larger classroom and is unsure whether the freedom of home study has taught her enough about managing externally imposed deadlines.

Life now

  • enjoys: Essays · Puzzle letters · Animal records
  • avoids: Livestock show grooming · Unexplained group rules
  • activities: Library discussion · Cooperative science · Children’s theater
  • demonstratedSkills: Detailed recordkeeping · Inventive word puzzles · Understands character motivations
  • unfamiliarActivities: Large classes · Frequent timed exams · Dormitory life
  • motivations: Testing her own opinions · Learning outside familiar circles
  • ambitions: Try a class with unfamiliar expectations · She imagines adulthood with open land nearby, lively conversations, and freedom to revise her plans.
  • struggles: External deadlines · Deference to confident speakers
  • supports: Parents · Cooperative tutor · Librarian · Theater friend
  • practicalConstraints: Rural travel · Need to document homeschool coursework

Still uncertain: How will she adapt to a larger class and fixed timetable? · Which family assumptions will she retain after wider exposure?
